utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to cross-examine the witness? May I draw your attention to the fact that as far as the 60 per cent guidance is concerned, a couple of times the Prosecution has taken more time at this moment. It's just to draw your attention to that, that it's not something that could continue. And then before you continue, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Kapetina, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration given at the beginning of your testimony, and I would also like to draw your attention to the following: When I re-read some of your answers yesterday where Mr. Tieger put certain things to you, you answered by saying: "Would you expect me to ignore the government," et cetera, et cetera. It took us some time to get to know what you exactly meant by that. If you would have said, "Mr. Tieger, your assumption is not right because I acted on the instructions of Mr. Simovic, who was at that time the one I received instructions from since Mr. Doko had left that to him," then in one or two lines you would have fully informed the Chamber about what your position was, and it would have been far more informative rather than asking Mr. Tieger what he would expect you to do. I do understand. It's to some extent also a consequence, perhaps, of the -- could I say the trial technique in which in cross-examination something is put to you and then you can respond. But as informative as you are, the better it is for the Chamber to fully understand your testimony. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Tieger: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kapetina. Toward the end of yesterday's session --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Toward the end of yesterday's session there was some discussion about the Council of Ministers. That body, is it correct, was established by the Bosnian Serb Assembly at its fourth session held on December 21, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably right. I don't remember the date exactly, but if you say so, then it probably is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall attending that session?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And after the establishment of the Council of Ministers and at its first session as reflected in the record of that session as we saw yesterday, the Council of Ministers determined, among other things, to provide for coordination with the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the Ministerial Council or Council of Ministers, so I don't know whether it had that task or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any reference to the -- to an interest by the Bosnian Serb leadership or representatives of the Bosnian Serbs to either of the December sessions of the Assembly that you attended in establishing connections to or coordination with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that coordination was supposed to be there anyway before the session and after the session. The JNA was the legitimate and legal part of the armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And by the same token, that cooperation should have been a continuous one, and not only after that particular session, and not only of the leadership of the SDS in the government but the whole institution of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it the answer to that question is, yes, you do recall such references at either or both Assembly sessions. Let me --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a guest at the Assembly, and that's how I behaved. Now, I can't remember what was discussed at the session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if your answer is you can't remember, that's your answer, sir. And speaking of that, let me turn --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's how it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn quickly to the document presented to you by the Defence, and that's the instructions of December 19, 1991, the Variant A and B document. I believe you said during your examination-in-chief in response to a question by Mr. Josse about the document that the first time you had ever seen it was when it was presented to you here in The Hague by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I had perhaps seen the document when I had an interview with the investigators of the OTP of this Tribunal. I didn't say that I saw the document in Sarajevo in 2004 -- or, rather, I think I remember seeing the document then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you're right, Mr. Kapetina. I misquoted and I was just checking that even before you began your answer. Your answer was to the question did you see this document around that time, in other words, in late 1991 or 1992, and I'm referring now to page 62 of the January 17th session. "The first time I saw this document was when I was interviewed by the investigators of the Prosecutor's office of this Tribunal." And your --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is correct that you were shown the document during the course of the July 2004 interview with the investigators of the Prosecution. But at that time, Mr. Kapetina, you said the following: It was presented to you, you were given an opportunity to look at it. In fact, the tape was shut off, and I'm now referring to page 62 of the January 17th interview. And five minutes later all -- the tape machine was turned back on and you were asked whether you had seen that document before, and you said, "It is possible that I saw it maybe at some municipality, but I did not have to use it. It was not delivered to me. That's it." And that's -- excuse me. That's at page 23 of the July 2004 interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take the other microphone for a second, Mr. Josse. It doesn't help that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's flashing -- a green flashing light rather than the normal red light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will have to ask the assistance of the interpreters. I hope that you're convinced that it's not the policy of this Tribunal to switch off microphones of Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I won't comment on that, Your Honour. But I've -- thank you very much. Thank you. The transcript said 17th of January. My fault. Yes. My learned friend said page 62, but the 17th of January interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. The confusion is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can sit down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The reference to Variant A and B during the course of the witness's examination-in-chief can be found at page 62 of the transcript of a couple of days ago, on the 17th, and the reference in the July 2004 interview as mentioned a few moments ago is at page 23.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, when you -- apparently when you had an opportunity to see the document in July of 2004, you acknowledged the possibility that you had seen it previously, and yet when you came to this Tribunal to testify you stated that the first time you had seen it was during the course of that interview. It appears to be the case from the two transcripts that you believed in July of 2004 that you might have seen the document before. Is that not in fact the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see it before.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain why you stated in July of 2004 when the document was presented to you and you were given a reasonable period of time to look it over that you believed that you had possibly seen it before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. I saw the document for the first time then, and since I didn't have much time and wasn't able to leaf through it, I had seen similar documents previously, but now I categorically state that that -- I saw that document the first time in the interview in July 2004.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn our attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, can I ask one question? When you say "similar documents," would you mean other copies of this document or -- I mean, would it be same number of pages, same text approximately, or would it be instructions but of a different kind? I'm just trying to understand what you mean by "similar documents."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't mean the same document, the very same document, but similar other documents by other people. Quite simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That clarifies your answer. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your examination-in-chief, you told us about your stay in Hadzici between March and May of 1992, and I believe you testified that you "volunteered in Hadzici with other intellectuals," and that reference, I think, can be found at page 58. Can you tell us whether a separate Serbian Assembly of Hadzici was formed in April of 1992 during the course of your work there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't work there. I said that as a volunteer, I became involved, but -- now, I don't know whether the Serbian Assembly was separated from the Municipal Assembly, but a meeting was organised, anyway, of all the Serbs in the Hadzici municipality, and the president of the Assembly for the Serbian municipality of Hadzici was elected and the council that I mentioned a moment ago numbering 20 people, 20 intellectuals. Now, I don't know what happened with the deputies who were legally elected at the elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a Crisis Staff of the Serbian people formed in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it was formed. I didn't have that kind of information, nor did I work in the staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it, then, you wouldn't know who -- if or who -- if there was a president of a Crisis Staff or who it was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether a separate Serbian TO was formed or prepared in April of 1992 while you were there as a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't work in those matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- can you tell us whether there was an intention by Bosnian Serb officials in Hadzici to have Serbian members of the TO coordinate with or work together with the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I wasn't their superior. I know that the commander of the Territorial Defence in Hadzici was a Muslim, and the secretary of the secretariat I seem to feel was a Serb, and they would be best placed to provide that kind of information, but I didn't contact them directly myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us as of early or mid-April of 1992 there was an intention by Bosnian Serb officials to form a separate Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that a police station was set up, but I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were there as a volunteer, did you participate in or hear about discussions concerning the intention to set it up, the fact that it had been set up, or the functioning of such a body?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which body?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about a separate Serbian police station or force.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard people that -- people talk about that at meetings. I attended some meetings, as did a group of sometimes five, sometimes more members of the council. They were intellectuals, as I say, from Hadzici, and for the most part the meetings were marathon meetings, very long, to talk about agreements, preserving the peace, and there was also mention of having the police separate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that the interest in having the police separate realised? Did it happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said a moment ago that a police station was formed of the Serbian people, as far as I understood it, and I wasn't involved directly in the negotiations about that, but the station was set up to have complete control over the Serb people in Hadzici to avoid having the Serb people create any excessive incidents. So this police station might have been formed to set up a fuller control over the Serbian population in Hadzici in which they were a minority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've heard testimony from another person from Hadzici who provided some information about the council or advisory body that you -- that you mentioned, and he testified that there was talk of forming a Crisis Staff at the founding Assembly. Do you remember that discussion, about the possibility of forming a Crisis Staff at the founding Assembly of the Serbian people in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there wasn't the mention of the formation of a Crisis Staff or I didn't pay enough attention, and I thought that the Assembly, and I think so now, was prepared by the Serbs and not by a political party at all. So all the Serbs, in actual fact, asked that a meeting be held to look into the situation, to see where things had escaped control, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also testified that the advisory -- council advisory body made a decision around April 24th to form the Crisis Staff. Does that refresh your recollection around the involvement of the council in the establishment of the Crisis Staff and the timing of the establishment of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that could have been on the 24th, because at the end of April I had already left Hadzici myself, and I don't know about this particular initiative and the formation of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to look quickly at two documents that are found in the Prosecution packet. The first is found at tab 10, and I'd like that marked with a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P1041.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm advised -- I didn't see it on my list -- this has a Defence number already. That's D110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the number P1041 is free again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just very quickly, Mr. Kapetina, if you'd look at D110. That's a list of those present at the Assembly of the Serbian People of Hadzici municipality on April 11th, 1992. And can you find your name at number 31, and does that conform with your recollection of your presence at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said I was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, I'd like you to look at tab 11, and I believe that does need a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 11 will be P1041, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P1041 reflect the minutes of a meeting of April 11th, 1992, of the council of the Serbian Municipal Assembly and advisory organ of the Hadzici Serb Municipal Assembly, and in addition to a list of names, it also contains an agenda and a reflection of the discussion that took place at that meeting. And can you see that discussion, Mr. Kapetina, and in particular, can you see your name found at the bottom of the portion that contains references to particular persons and comments they made?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but -- it's a very poor copy, difficult to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree, and I appreciate that certain portions may be difficult to read. I'll just try to direct your attention to those that are in fact legible. First of all, we see toward the top that Ratko Radic speaks and indicates that the Serbian TO and an army unit may act together. The Serbian population needs to be protected from all possible attacks. And if you go toward the bottom of the page, just two people up from yourself, Veljko Banduka says: "The Serbian TO is already being organised into military units and there is cooperation with the units," and I believe the rest is illegible. Doesn't that reflect the existence of and the activities of the Serbian TO by April 11, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that piece of information. But let me add this: People don't know, are not well-versed in the system of defence. They heard that some sort of Territorial Defence existed and some sort of JNA, but they didn't actually have any knowledge about that. And they very often say a lot of nonsense at these meetings and propose things that are not quite illogical and not reasonable. So these are arbitrary discussions on the part of people who never had any knowledge about what national defence meant. And we will see that later on. People think they know everything very often, and then they tell some tales about the JNA and bodies like this, but they don't really have any knowledge about what this means, and I'd like the Trial Chamber to realise that, because people don't have sufficient knowledge and information and not the right professional information and legal information about all these things. So people can go to a meeting and say what they like. But it's not a document and it's not a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm a little confused then, Mr. Kapetina. I thought you had described yourself as being relatively uninvolved in events in Hadzici and yet I now understand you to be telling the Court that the reference, the specific references here during the course of this meeting are not to be trusted because you know better than the people who were talking. So which is it? Were you involved enough to be able to say whether or not there was a Serbian TO, or were you sufficiently uninvolved that you'd have to defer to others who purport to know about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before you continue, could you please indicate exactly where the witness said not in general terms that people would often speak about matters they hardly had any knowledge about but that in this specific respect the speakers during this meeting were speaking without knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I misunderstood, Your Honour. I asked the witness if his reference to -- if his -- what the Court has described is a reference in general terms to people who speak without knowledge was a reference to these speakers who were talking about the Serbian TO. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness said: "And I didn't know about that piece of information. But let me add this: People don't know, are not well-versed in the system of defence, and they usually say a lot of nonsense. It's all in very general terms."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "So these are arbitrary discussions. It was not one arbitrary discussion but arbitrary discussions." I think the witness explained to us that people are often speaking without knowledge. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, in light of --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're just cautioning us not based on your own knowledge of what was happening in Hadzici but as a general matter to -- that you have found that people sometimes speak without sufficient knowledge. Is that basically it, as the Court understood it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I couldn't correct everybody. I couldn't tell everybody how this should function, how things should be done or shouldn't be done, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say: "I couldn't correct everyone." Are you now -- "I couldn't correct everybody. I couldn't tell everybody how this should function ..." Are you now again speaking in general terms or are you referring to that meeting? What are you telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In more specific terms, when we're talking about this meeting, they -- I can't see my name in the first list. As far as I can see, it is not there. Maybe I joined the meeting later, because in this list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's another matter. I think your name appears on the document, even if it's not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying here, I may not even have heard all the -- the interventions, all that was said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which draws your attention, Mr. Tieger, to another matter, which is the following: That on the list of those attending, it appears that -- at least I read that there was a Cedo Kapetina. Whereas in the agenda we have one reference to Cedo Kapetina, and that's the one I think you referred to, whereas Dragan Kapetina appears at the very end which you did not refer to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, can you turn to item 12 of the Prosecution packet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can that be given a new number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 12 will be P1042, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P1042 is an announcement to the Serbian people of Hadzici municipality. It's -- it bears the names at the end of the president of the working Presidency, Ratko Radic; the secretary of the Assembly, Ratko Gengo; the president of the Assembly of the Serb People, Drago Milosevic; and the vice-president of the Assembly of the Serb People in Hadzici, Dragan Kapetina. It indicates after the preparatory language concerning the difficult political security situation the election of those persons and in item 2 some of the decisions passed by the Assembly of the Serb People in Hadzici, including the decision on the creation of a Serb police station, the appointment of its chief, and a decision on the appointment of the Serbian people's TO staff with Milo Bratic appointed Staff Commander. Is this an announcement, Mr. Kapetina, that you, Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Gengo, and Mr. Radic prepared or had prepared and disseminated to the Serbian people of Hadzici municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the date on this announcement. Do you have any indication as to when this was drafted? Could you do that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Item 1 says the Assembly of the Serb People in Hadzici municipality constituted the organs and bodies of the Assembly of the Serb People in Hadzici municipality at its meeting on 11 April 1992 and they are as follows, and goes on to indicate the passage of the items I just referred to.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked this because I can see that this announcement was not signed by the individuals indicated here. I'm not aware of this announcement. I suppose that this announcement was printed and disseminated after I left Hadzici. I don't know when the announcement was written. I know that there is a reference to the Assembly and when it was set up, but I don't know why these people did not sign this announcement. This announcement may have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, you have drawn our attention to the fact that it is undated and it may have been issued after you left. Any more questions, Mr. Tieger, about the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The call on the document for all Serb conscripts to register with the Serbian TO, it would appear to be something of a time-sensitive matter. Wouldn't you agree, Mr. Kapetina? It would be something that the Serbian officials of Hadzici would be anxious to disseminate as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My intervention went to the date and the signatures, because I don't remember an announcement of this sort. If I could remember this announcement, I would provide you with an explanation. That's why I wanted to know the date, because it is quite likely that I was no longer there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, I think Mr. Tieger is interested to know whether you have any recollection that on the 11th of April that you were elected vice-president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That on that date did the Assembly take a decision on the creation of a Serb police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At that Assembly, no decision on a police station was taken. This happened later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I did not participate in the negotiations concerning the police, but I know that at the Assembly the president and the vice-president of the Assembly were appointed, and the President of the Executive Board was confirmed, the person who had been in that position before, and also the heads of the Serbian bodies that had already been in their positions, and the council was established, nothing else. Whatever is mentioned here in this announcement happened later, after the 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you know that it happened at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because the police station was established already when I was there, and I've already told you that. This was not a new police station, you have to understand. Quite simply, the Serbian staff leave one room and move to another room, and that's how the police station was established. It was not an entirely new institution. I don't want to go into the reasons why this happened, but in simple terms this was not a newly established institution. In simple terms, the existing police station was divided into a Serbian police station and a Muslim police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did that, then, exactly happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After this Assembly. The Assembly took place on the 12th. Then this happened between the 12th and the 30th of April. And I can tell you exactly what the cause of this division was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The high official of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian MUP was driving a lorry of arms across Mount Igman to Sarajevo. He was being escorted by the police from Hadzici. On Mount Igman, he was intercepted by the Serbian policemen who arrested him with a lorry full of arms. And after that date there was a lot of mistrust among the policemen. But this was not the only case. Such cases happened across Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I believe that there is an Official Note on this incident. This was reported on the media. I can't remember the name of this high official, but he was assistant minister of the interior, and he was escorting a lorry full of arms across Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was a Mr. Glavas ever chief of a Serb police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was the police commander previously in the former police station. He was legally appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, yesterday there was discussion about communications which I'm sure and you the Court will recall. Let me ask you a couple of questions about communications in 1992. First of all, is it correct that the army and the Main Staff had their own communication systems and centres?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had them early on. They may have had only military communication systems. At the beginning, they did not have centres. In May they did -- in May they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the Ministry of Interior? Did it have its own communication centres?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember. The ministry existed in various places. I don't know when they moved to Bijeljina. I can't tell you because I don't have that information. I was the last to arrive in Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the Ministry of Defence? Did it have communication centres?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence ministry did have a communication centre in Pale. This is the centre that already existed before in Pale municipality, and it was just transformed into the communication centre in Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it true that in fact both the army and Main Staff had their own communication centres, the Ministry of Interior did, and that these communication centres, with their communication devices, never stopped working and were working when you arrived in Pale in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the centre belonging to the Ministry of Defence worked in Pale. I don't know about the others. I really don't know about the military. The military did not even exist when I arrived in Pale. The military was established on the 12th of May. What I'm referring to is the decision on its establishment. And it was actually established towards the end of May and the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked basically this same series of questions during the July 2004 interview, and I'm referring to pages 51 through 53 of that interview. And in particular during the -- toward the latter part of that discussion the question was asked: "I trust that the army and the Main Staff had their own communications with various corps." Your answer was: "Of course it has -- it had. It had its own communication centres, it had its own codes, its own documents." "Question: Just like the Ministry of Interior had its own communication between the CSBs and they had communication with the SJBs." Your answer: "Yes, yes, exactly." "Question: When you arrived in May of 1992, was most of the communications equipment up and running and working?" Your answer was: "Yeah, those communication devices never stopped working." Comment "okay" by the investigator. And then you said: "Those were centres, communication centres from the previous systems, and Bosnia-Herzegovina had the regional centres just like later on. What now ended up under control of Republika Srpska continued to work for Republika Srpska and in the same way worked for the other side. It wasn't something that was done afresh and had to be done now." Does that correctly reflect what you said, Mr. Kapetina, and was that a correct response?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me very specifically when I arrived in Pale on the 10th of May, and when I spoke to the investigators, I answered general questions, whether there was communication in the military, in the MUP. I don't remember that the investigators mentioned a very specific date or a very specific period. Every municipality had a communication centre, but how far that reached, that's a problem. Every municipality had its centre for its own territory, but the question is whether the systems of communications functioned at all. I'm referring to the telephone and telex lines. And there were such periods when they were not up and running. I answered a very general question as to whether everybody had their communications, and of course the answer was yes. But when those communications were established and whether they functioned, it's a different story. Very often there was no electricity. There was no oil for 15 or 20 days. For example, communications could be down for 15 or 20 days because there was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, I'll say once again in case -- in the course of reminding you what was said on that occasion I didn't focus on the -- a specific question and answer: "Question: When you arrived in May of 1992, was most of the communications equipment up and running and working?" "Answer: Yeah, those communication devices never stopped working." That would seem to direct your attention specifically to May 1992, and your answer would seem to cover that period and the period thereafter as well. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've tried to explain just now. Having equipment is one thing, but the range of that equipment is a different story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, at this moment we're not exploring the communications, but Mr. Tieger was exploring what he considers to be an inconsistency between the statement you gave and the testimony you've given in this -- you've just given where you said no specific question as far as the date was put to me, whereas Mr. Tieger draws your attention to the fact that the question was specifically about the moment of your arrival in -- in May in Pale. Does that change anything in the answer you've given until now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer doesn't change, and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, you testified in response to questions by the Defence about the Presidency of Republika Srpska in 1992. You never attended meetings of the Presidency in 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never were provided with or read minutes of the meetings of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those minutes, there was no duty to deliver them to the Ministry of Defence. So if there was no such duty, then of course I did not read them. Maybe only if at a Presidency meeting a task was issued to the minister of defence. Otherwise, those minutes did not have to be delivered to the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it you don't recall ever reading minutes of the Presidency in 1992 yourself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the -- what you explained as the chronology of the variations of that office in 1992. You said that there was, first, a three-member Presidency, then a Presidency with one president and two vice-presidents. And finally: "When Republika Srpska was established, the president of the republic was appointed." Now, I take it, Mr. Kapetina, that you don't recall the specific constitutional provisions or legal provisions reflecting those bodies or the specific dates on which they were enacted, or do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I have read the constitution and the laws, and I do that still, but I don't retain any of that in my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if those constitutional provisions or other legal provisions relating to those bodies reflect a different chronology or composition, would you defer to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be discrepancies. However, at the beginning there was a Presidency. After the Presidency, a president and two vice-presidents composing a body. There may have been a third thing in addition to those two, but I don't know. I don't know what you're referring to in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that answer is quite sufficient, Mr. Kapetina. Let me turn now to -- briefly to an issue you raised yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I remind you about the 60 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Court can be assured I have that in mind. I have been attempting to move as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm not saying you're not moving quickly, but how much time would you still need, do you expect?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would think no more than 15 minutes, and I think that's -- I hope to be finished faster than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would please do so, because the Chamber would very much like to go into private session before the next break, because it's not impossible that certain matters would have to be done during the next break as a result of going into private session. Therefore, could you please finish within the next eight or nine minutes, of course depending on the direct responses to your answers -- to your questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, yesterday you told us about a report by an assistant or deputy minister of justice concerning prisons. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be the report by Slobodan Avlijas, the deputy minister of justice, that was commissioned by the government on August 9, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this report was drafted by Slobodan Avlijas. I don't know whether he was deputy or assistant. I know that he was assistant, but that doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was commissioned in the wake of an international outcry about the -- about Omarska after journalists had gained access; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why the government wanted to have this report. I could not follow the work of the minister of justice as well as of the minister of defence. The Ministry of Justice had just been established and they drafted this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weren't you at the August 9th meeting of the government at which that commission -- at which that commission was formed and tasked, or which that report was tasked to the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have been, but I was there to act on behalf the Ministry of Defence and to submit the reports on the work of the Ministry of Defence. I was not a member of the government, and I was not involved in all the issues. When I was invited to a session, I acted on behalf of the defence minister, and I presented issues that had to do with defence, exclusively with defence, and I didn't even have the right of decision at any of those sessions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't recall any discussion related to the Omarska camp, to the international outcry surrounding that camp, and to the establishment of -- to the decision to form -- to have a report about prisons and camps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I know that that report was discussed at the government session. As for the cause, why this report was commissioned, I don't know. Maybe I was absent from the session when that issue was discussed. I don't have all the information about that. It was a long time ago. It's very difficult for me to remember all the things that happened at that time. There were two government sessions taking place within the space of seven days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know about a government order or request for a report by the minister of justice on prisoners with specific attention to the treatment of both civilians and prisoners of war, a request in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the detailed request made of the government -- by the government of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You were not aware of the detailed request. Were you aware generally of a request by the government or an order by the government to the Ministry of Justice for a report on prisoners with specific attention to the treatment of civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I did hear of a request like that. I heard that the -- that the government considered a report, but I don't know about a request, because I assume the government sent out a request to a specific department, not to all the departments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know about the establishment of a working group to consider that issue?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you know that the government considered a report. Was that a report in June of 1992 that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably that first report. If it was the first report, then that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the results of that report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the issue of prisoners or confinement of civilians was ever raised at this Assembly of the Bosnian People -- Bosnian Serb people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Kapetina, I'd like to turn to one last tab. That's tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'd like to give it a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 20, Your Honours, will be P1043.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, P1043 is a newspaper report of May 13, 1998, reporting that a Bosnian Serb leader, in that case Mr. Krajisnik, as the article goes on to say, was accused in parliament of violating the Dayton Peace Accords and plotting to return hard-liners to power in the Bosnian Serb entity. It goes on to say that Mr. Krajisnik hired the former chief of staff General Pero Colic and yourself while planning to hire around 20 other former military officials as advisors, according to Defence Minister Milovanovic. And the article, as you can see, goes on to say that the defence minister accused Mr. Krajisnik and his ultra nationalist supports of wanting to "create paramilitary and police institutions aimed at recovering power in Republika Srpska." Were you in fact hired by Mr. Krajisnik along with General Colic as an advisor during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik never hired me as his advisor, never. Just while working in the Ministry of Defence as deputy minister, I performed the function in the permanent committee for military matters, but I was never employed in the Assembly, in the National Assembly of Republika Srpska. And everything that it says here are pure lies. This man must be drunk rather than a normal person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about General Colic? Do you know whether or not he was an advisor to Mr. Krajisnik during that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about General Colic either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And does it change your answer at all that the -- to refer you to the portion of the article that indicates that at that time Mr. Krajisnik was a member of the Bosnian Presidency rather than being hired specifically -- rather than referring to anyone's retention as an advisor in the capacity of Assembly president?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those are precisely the things that I was talking about. People have no idea what the Presidency means, what the president is. This man has absolutely no idea of what post Krajisnik had at the time. He was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's what he said. But when this report came out, statement came out, Mr. Krajisnik was a president -- a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not the Presidency of Republika Srpska at all, as far as I remember, of course. So quite simply, this entire passage are pure fabrications and lies, and it's not the first time that this man has done that. He came before the Assembly of Republika Srpska and spoke such nonsense that the deputies asked the Premier to have him come to his senses, help him come to his senses and sober up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour. Mr. Josse, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to begin, I'm going to seek now to put in the whole of this witness's interview with the Office of the Prosecutor. Well, my learned friend rises. I'm going to need to develop my argument. And I want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would say that he didn't disagree with you. He didn't object. No. Let's proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm in your hands, Your Honour. There are quite significant passages that I wish to take him through in re-examination. But Your Honour might want to hear the legal argument first of all, because I suspect that's going to take a little bit of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- assuming that Mr. Tieger would object if not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think you can assume that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any -- then please develop your arguments so that Mr. Tieger can respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the presence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should that be done in the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He should not be in the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He should not be in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution. I'm content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Kapetina, you are invited to follow Madam Usher since a procedural matter has to be discussed. Would you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The exercise I wish to carry out falls into two distinct parts. The first is I want to put in front of the witness the interview. I appreciate that it's in English, and clearly we will need to go through it very slowly. I want to go through all three passages that my learned friend put to him, invite him to look at them, bits before, bits afterwards, and then invite comments as we go through them as to the answers that he was given. That, beyond a shadow of a doubt, arises from the cross-examination of my learned friend. Secondly, I submit that the whole interview is now admissible before this Court. This witness, having been cross-examined in terms as to inconsistency by my learned friend in relation to three different passages, the rest of the interview is now admissible as to his consistency. Clearly inconsistency having been put into question by the Prosecution, consistency is a matter the Defence can deal with in the course of re-examination. Thirdly, and extremely significantly, it is not without -- it is not a coincidence, we contend, that the Prosecution have not included this document in their bundle. These Prosecutors, with all due respect to them, prosecute this case with great caution. They also prepare their cross-examination with great diligence, and I don't mean that in the least bit ironically. They made a conscious decision, in my submission, not to put this document in their bundle. Let's take a look. Mr. Tieger has done me a great turn --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can Your Honour excuse me. I don't want to interrupt, but before this argument is pursued much further I think it's fair to say that the interviews are present. They are effectively part of the bundle. They were here in court, prepared to be disseminated. It's' just for logistical reasons you can't put them together there, but they've been here the entire time. So I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll accept that. I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's continue that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll accept that. I'll accept that and withdraw what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But by way of contrast, and the point I was coming to is still, I hope, one that I can make. Let's look at the last document, tab 20. Tab 20 has just been put to this witness. It contains, I needn't tell the Court, a press report of something a man called Milanovic, as it happens, is alleged to have said at an Assembly about this witness and about Mr. Krajisnik. That's in the bundle that the Court have. But what the Court don't have are the very pertinent words that this witness uttered in the course of a very long interview both in May and July of last year conducted by the Prosecution. If this document, tab 20, by way of example, and it's simply by way of example of the way cross-examination is conducted with permission in this Court is admitted into evidence, why on earth, I contend, is the interview not admitted into evidence? It's clearly far more pertinent, far more relevant and of far more use in a fact-finding exercise than tab 20. And I emphasise tab 20 is just by way of example. It's the way cross-examination is conducted. As I've already said, it's conducted in a diligent and proper way under the Rules of this Tribunal. And in my submission, bearing in mind the cross-examination of this particular witness in particular, as I've already said, the fact that my learned friend has gone through three separate passages, the whole of the interview is now admissible. But, Your Honour, just to recap, my submission in fact is in two parts. First of all, that the Court must be entitled now to see the three passages that have been cross-examined upon, what went before them and what went after them, but I submit the cross-examination now permits the admission of the whole interview to show consistency as against the inconsistency that my learned friend understandably has relied upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, let's focus first on -- I think Mr. Josse started saying that the witness should be in a position to comment on his statement not only the lines you quoted but also little bit before, a little bit after that so to give us comment in a more contextual -- his comment in a more contextual way; and then the second one that since you have found inconsistencies that the Defence would like to demonstrate that it's I take it mainly consistent with his testimony given in this court. Let's focus on that first. What are then your objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, with respect to the issue of the context of cited passages, there's nothing new here, and we've addressed that issue before, and of course I don't have any intention of inventing new rules for either this particular proceeding or for the institution generally. We've established this ground rule earlier. And if there is a particular portion which is appropriate for the passages cited and is contextually appropriate, as we have done in the past, that's -- that's a perfectly appropriate course, and I would want the context, if it is indeed context, that bears on that particular passage to be available, either to the witness, or to the Court, or both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you broadening a bit of the passages I confronted the witness with is not a problem for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And then the second issue consistency/inconsistency by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, there's a few problems with that, Your Honour. Number one, it's logically flawed. The notion that somehow if the witness is inconsistent about something elicited by the Defence during examination-in-chief that that can somehow be rehabilitated by the fact that he was consistent on other matters is untenable. There is no relationship between the two. If the Defence elicits testimony and the witness has previously said something inconsistent with that, that doesn't change even if a -- if he was consistent about other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Number two, it's a circumvention of the Rules, or is an attempted circumvention of the Rules. So they want -- there are time limits to everybody and everything. Now suddenly the Defence would like to get in a huge amount of material without the opportunity for the Prosecution to cross-examine that was neither listed in the 65 ter, that was not the subject of any notice of intention to lead and was not -- no cross-examination was prepared for that purpose, and that effectively circumvents and subverts the time limits imposed for the case generally. But number three, and I think in some respects most compelling, is this issue's already been addressed earlier during the course of the Prosecution case, and it was a position taken by the Defence. They certainly had no interest in seeing entire interviews for the most part simply provided. Now, I know entire interviews were provided on occasion by agreement between the parties when there was reason to do so, but as a general matter it was not available to the Prosecution simply to place in evidence entire portions -- entire transcripts of previous examinations and previous interviews. In fact, there was some fairly tightly circumscribed rules pertaining to the ability even to impeach witnesses on portions of those. So for a variety of reasons, Your Honour, I submit that it's not an appropriate submission and would oppose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, I would specifically like to hear your response to the argument raised by Mr. Tieger saying that the remainder of the interview is not in the 65 ter, and I stood -- understood his argument to be, but it's my interpretation, that if you confront a witness with those portions of his testimony in chief, limited portions that are in the 65 ter or at least are close to the 65 ter summary, that if on the basis of that testimony to test the credibility and reliability of the witness, you would on those specific portions confront him with what Mr. Tieger considers inconsistencies with his previous statements, would that open the whole of the just in order to establish consistency on other matters, matters perhaps that have not been dealt with at all in the examination-in-chief, and also in view of the -- in view of the argument by Mr. Tieger that three inconsistencies cannot be cured by a full consistent story of the remainder. I also would like to draw the attention, not only your attention but also Mr. Tieger's attention, to the type of inconsistency, especially if a witness says, "I could not exclude the possibility that I've seen this document before," and if he later says, "I haven't seen it," is that an inconsistency, yes or no? That's -- and if it is an inconsistency, what is the importance of that inconsistency? And I'm saying this because the inconsistencies were -- well, let's -- let me same the following: I've seen greater inconsistencies during the examination of witnesses in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I deal with the last point first. That was my learned friend's decision. He took the risk. He chose to cross-examine on the basis of inconsistency. In a common law system, if an advocate does that, puts a portion of an interview in this fashion to the witness or a portion of what he said previously, then he stands the risk of the re-examining party getting up and saying, Well, the rest of what you said is consistent with your testimony. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first -- could I ask you, is that in dispute? Mr. Tieger, is the remainder -- do you -- is it the position of the Defence that these inconsistencies - you pointed at the three - that they are an illustration of inconsistency of this testimony in general terms with the statement of the witness, or would you say, "I pointed at the three inconsistencies I found and I did not find any other inconsistencies"? Perhaps some of what he said has not been dealt with at all, but then at least you do not find any inconsistency. You understand what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean -- I want to see whether how to resolve this matter. And, Mr. Josse, we need the whole of it in order to demonstrate that he was consistent in other respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It is showing or pointing to an inconsistency on particular point is not a way saying that when he previously spoke in general about many, many subjects that he was inconsistent on all of those. Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. And is -- if Mr. Josse wants to use the whole of the interview to demonstrate that apart from the three matters you raised that he can demonstrate to the Chamber that there are no further inconsistencies found, is that something that would be in dispute? Would you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm pretty much stuck with the position that if I haven't pointed to an inconsistency I'm not in a very good position to argue that the witness was inconsistent on another point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just -- just trying to find out to what extent Mr. Josse says, I want the whole of the interview in order to take away any impression that the witness was any further inconsistent than raised by the Prosecution up to this moment. My question is, is that in dispute; or would you say, no, apart from the three points, I did not find any consistencies -- inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I mean essentially -- I mean to say, as I understand it, and I hope I'm not missing something here, that I'm not in a position to assert that the witness was inconsistent in those interviews on any other point. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Because I didn't raise them. I didn't point them out. So how could the Prosecution then assert that he was inconsistent in the previous interview without any basis for doing so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, so now we are at the point where you say the witness -- I wanted to show the witness was consistent in the remainder of his interview compared with his testimony, and Mr. Tieger says, "I could not possibly argue that there were any further inconsistencies than I have seen." So it seems that the parties are in agreement on the remainder. Mr. Tieger, perhaps from lack of knowledge of not having demonstrated it and you perhaps by conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, he has not conceded that the witness was consistent for the rest of the interview. The negative will not do in these circumstances, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I do understand your point. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I go back to Your Honour's first point just raised, namely in relation to the 65 ter. It had crossed my mind to at one point submit the whole of the interview, which of course was served on us under Rule 68 as our 65 ter. That, I suspect, would have been deemed a cheap trick and with some justification. And -- but I would invite the Court to bear in mind, and whilst I accept that this isn't quite the same principle, that the Prosecution for one reason or another were able to introduce large parts of their evidence under 89(F) saving everyone a great deal of time. Now, the position is, as I say, for one reason or another, we certainly hitherto have not been in a position to do that. We're unlikely, save perhaps for one or two witnesses, to be able to do that very much. And it is bearing in mind the overall justice of the situation something the Court might want to bear in mind in terms of any additional matters that are raised in the course of this interview. By the same token, Your Honour is quite capable, no doubt, of putting a line through any part of this interview that Your Honour thinks is not fair on the Prosecution, doesn't in any way assist the case as I suspect Your Honour does with a great deal of the evidence, a great number of the exhibits perhaps I should say, that are placed before the Court. They may not be realised, but they're notionalised simply saying, We ignore that passage, it hasn't been dealt with sufficiently properly, it's of no interest to us, and so on and so forth. So this Court, this Court of professional Judges is quite capable of, in my submission, making the distinction between those parts that are relevant and those parts that are irrelevant, those parts that are properly admissible, those parts that are properly inadmissible. And so in my submission, the position isn't the way Mr. Tieger presents it. And as I say, the fair course, I submit, particularly I repeat the point I've made before, bearing in mind the sort of documents that do go in in the course of cross-examination, it's not unreasonable for the Defence now in the light of the cross-examination of Mr. Kapetina to ask for the whole of this interview to be admitted into evidence. Finally, so far as what went before, most of the argument, I can't promise all of it. I have a note of some of the previous arguments in terms of interviews that have taken place in this case. Most of the argument related to witnesses whom the Prosecution called, whom the Prosecution asserted were hostile witnesses, and it was the Prosecution who wanted to put large passages of their own witness' interviews before the Court on the basis, as Mr. Tieger said at some point to this Court, that they hadn't been proofed by the Prosecution because in effect they were hostile. This is completely different in my submission. The Defence are now seeking to put this interview in as a result of the cross-examination of the -- of the opposing party, namely Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I may remind you, Mr. Josse, is that of course whenever any document was admitted that always an opportunity was given to the Defence to carefully study it and to make redactions, and very often this Chamber followed the redactions in those statements. But the Chamber will consider whether and if so to what extent the Chamber will admit the whole of the interview. Could I just learn about how many pages there are in that interview? I mean, are we talking about 20 or a hundred?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One interview is 68. The other interview is 40 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 66 okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 134, Your Honour, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 25 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will first give its ruling on the application by the Defence to admit into evidence the whole of the interview. The Chamber admits the whole of the interview in evidence for the sole purpose that has been given by Mr. Josse. That means that those portions Mr. Tieger confronted the witness with, that it's clear that the purpose of confronting him with it was about inconsistency. Mr. Josse, you will have an opportunity to go beyond what Mr. Tieger confronted the witness with. Then as far as the remainder of that document is concerned, to the extent that the interview deals with matters which are in the testimony of this witness, the Chamber will use that document in order to see whether it can positively establish consistency with the testimony given in court. Everything that has not -- is of -- has not been raised during the testimony, the Chamber will not use that as a basis for establishing facts which may be contained in those portions of the statement on which the Prosecution hasn't had an opportunity to cross-examine the witness. That's the ruling of the Chamber. So it is admitted into evidence, but the purpose of admission into evidence is, I hope, entirely clear now to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's clear to me, Your Honour, and the Court will be glad to hear that I'm only going to re-examine on two passages and then I've got one or two other short questions in re-examination. I'm not going to go through with the witness all those parts that are consistent with his evidence. I'll have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll be able to read that and to see to what extent it covers the matters raised. Mr. Tieger, I hardly dare to ask you whether you understood it, but I only do it because I might have been unclear on the purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I believe understand the Court's ruling. I'm a little perplexed about how the parties are to know what portions will be ultimately available for citation or unavailable for citation in later portions of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there is any question about that, and if one of the parties would like to know about it, you can seek the guidance of the Court. So we'll consider that even previous to -- if one party says, Is this something you considered in establishing positively whether there's any consistency, yes or no, we'll give you that answer. So if there's any reason for you to know what exactly -- what portions the Chamber considers to cover matters that have been raised in -- in the examination of the witness, the Chamber -- the parties could seek guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honour, and also simply -- it maybe goes without saying, maybe it doesn't, reserve the opportunity to consider both the ruling and the implications of the ruling and perhaps raise it at later time if there is anything pertinent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of course if for any other reason at a later stage other portions of that statement that you would like to introduce that in evidence but for totally different reasons, then of course the Chamber will hear what your argument is at that time. But as it stands now, these are the limited purposes of admitting the whole of the interview into evidence. Then, Mr. Josse, are you ready so that we could ask the witness to be brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I am, and I'll hand out the interviews in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we first invite the registrar to give numbers to the documents. Let's take them in chronological order. Interview, 13th of July 2004, would be, Mr. Registrar -- I think a D number would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D121, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then 14th of May, 2004 will be 122.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Josse, you may proceed. Re-examined by Mr. Josse:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a little bit more, Mr. Kapetina, about this interview. The difficulty that you face is that though the interview was of course conducted in both English and B/C/S, the transcript that is now being handed out is only in English, as I think you're aware. It's fair to say, isn't it, that the investigators very properly gave you a CD containing the contents of the interview which you took home with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I took home was a cassette covering one day of interview. However, I was never provided with another second cassette covering the second day of the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could look, but the Court at least to look at the interview dated the 13th of July. Mr. Tieger asked some questions about page 14 of that interview, and you were asked a question: Did you send an identical report to the prime minister, the corps commander, and the TO commander? And your reply was -- the interpreter wasn't clear there, and so I'm going to go on. You answered: "I don't think so." And then you said: "And if I did send them, if I did send something to them, then it was just an information because I really did not cooperate with them, and I did not. They were not under me, but I think I did not send anything like that to them." What do you now say about that answer, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't send them a written caution, but I explained yesterday that it is possible that those institutions and heads of those institutions had received a caution and an invitation to attend a meeting of the Council for National Defence. That's why I said that they may have been provided with information, but I was not the one who sent that information to them because I was not duty-bound to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like now to turn, if we may, to page 23, and this passage we're going to look at, if we may, in a little bit more detail. And it's right I can summarise the top of the page as we've already heard, the interviewer put the document known in this Court as the Variant A and B document to you. You were given five minutes to read it. You were asked whether you've ever seen it before. And you said: "It is possible that I saw it, maybe at some municipality, but I did not have to use it. It was not delivered to me that." You then denied actually drafting or writing -- I beg your pardon. You were then asked whether you had written or drafted the manual, and it was at that point that you were shown the manual that is -- I think it's tab 1 of -- excuse me. It is tab 1 of the binder that has been presented to this Court by the Defence in the course of your evidence. And again summarising matters, you actually asked for a copy because you'd lost it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked for a copy of my own manual that the investigators showed to me. I did not have a single copy of my manual. That's why I asked to be provided with one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And simple yes would have done, Mr. Kapetina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then at the bottom of the page 23, you confirm that you'd written the manual. You give some answers about it which the Court can read perhaps at its leisure. And then turning the page, the top of page 24, you were asked about any similarities between your publication and the plans for extraordinary circumstances in the document I just showed you. And you said, and I'll read this slowly: "Mostly not, not even by coincidence. If you analyse this manual, then you will see that you can see over here that everything is done according to structure like every subject is. Everything is analysed according to structure, and everything over here is based on laws and regulations, so it's not based on my personal assumptions. It's based on law. But this is a public document, and everybody who wanted it could have used it. This is not the only work that I had that was published." Was that a truthful answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if I could go, again in the interests of time as much as anything else, to the bottom of page 24. You were asked the following question: "So where did they get the documents from? Do you have any idea who have been involved in drafting it?" This is a reference, I think, again to the Variant A and B document. "That document that was made by SDS, and that was in accordance with one plan that was present in all bodies, and it was present in the plan for defence of subjects and plans for and had the title like a plan of readiness, and the plan had certain steps and the plan of readiness had JNA units." And you go on and describe, I'm going to summarise this here, the type of planning that really existed in the old Yugoslavia and that this document fitted in to that scheme of things. Is that an accurate assessment of what you said or an accurate summary of what you said to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry, but maybe I'm not fully understanding this new system, but I thought it was to make clear what the witness had said. I guess -- if this is -- this portion is in evidence, then I won't bother to repeat it for the record, but it's clearly not a full summary of the answer, which concludes the line, "So the SDS leadership could have also used the form of that kind of planning."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems, Mr. Josse, that where you are seeking the further context of what Mr. Tieger raised, Mr. Tieger now in return wants to get the further context of what you raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I -- can I deal with it like this: I thought -- I asked a few questions. I'm unsurprisingly content with Your Honour's ruling. Based on that ruling, the document is now before the Court for its consideration subject to the rider that Your Honour has given. So far as the interview is concerned, I don't seek to ask any further questions. I accept what Mr. Tieger has said. The Court needs to read the whole of the answer in order to assess it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this now for consistency purposes that you have drawn our attention to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just consistency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tieger, it's clear that if you want to get anything more out of that you'll have to further ask questions about that. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you, please, to turn to the Prosecution bundle of exhibits and to tab 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 6 is P1040.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in particular, could you turn to paragraph 11, the last page on the B/C/S, the penultimate page in the English. This was put to you in the course of cross-examination. It relates to this note from the meeting of officials and top-ranking personnel of republican state organs, members of the SDS, Bosnia-Herzegovina, propose the establishment, it says, at number 11, "of a system of duty shifts to monitor the activities, an execution of tasks and the operation of state organs, resolution of existing problems in the various fields, and maintaining contacts with" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please read a bit slower. Thank you very much.
