utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Ljubisav Terzic and Dragan Kapetina are entrusted with this and the development of a means of communication between SDS and SDS personnel in republican state organs with the municipalities." I want to first ask you, bearing in mind what's said there, the extent to which the SDS put you into your job as Chief Inspector.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I think that this wording is due to the fact that Ljubisav Terzic, who was a member of the Ministerial Council, proposed that I should be in charge of this task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Try and answer my questions. We'll come back perhaps to the document in a moment. You were Chief Inspector in the ministry, you've told us that; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've told us you took that job or were appointed to it prior to the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the SDS have any part in getting you that job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was appointed to that duty, I believe that the SDS may have existed but it was not in power. So it was not the SDS that put my name to that duty. I was appointed by the previous Communist government, the Executive Council of Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not its government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that in those elections in 1990 you in fact stood for the SDP party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what extent did the SDS support you in keeping the job after the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they just supported me in that duty, which means that they did not propose any other person to fill that position in my stead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand that they expected anything in return?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's been suggested that you were an SDS lackey when you wrote the letter that you've told us about. What do you say to that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My final question is this: In the course of your evidence yesterday, you were giving an answer where you talked about Mr. Mesic, and at some point, and I, if need be, can tell you the context, you were talking about the fact that Oslobodjenje was partial, as was other media, that there was a general propaganda campaign so that writing of the media doesn't mean much. And you said: "I can remind you of another statement of Mr. Mesic when he completed his term of office, when he said, 'I have completed my task. Yugoslavia is no more.'" . And I think you were then interrupted in the answer you were given. Could you tell the Court what it is you were going to say about this statement by Mr. Mesic, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I was going to say is that other statements issued by Mr. Mesic could have been presented here to the Trial Chamber, which are -- were all part of the goal when he was appointed to that position, and the goal was to make Yugoslavia disappear. That was the goal, and the statements that may have been presented were with that goal in mind. And this was also part of the context -- overall context of other questions put to -- put by the Prosecution. But what I'm saying is that whatever information Oslobodjenje published quoting the Presidency is not correct, because the Presidency very often quoted both the Federal Executive Council and the Presidency and they sent false reports. I don't have any arguments to corroborate that. I don't have any documents to corroborate that, although there are documents to that effect. They informed the Presidency and the Federal Executive Council in a biased manner on what was going on on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The situation on the ground and what information they sent did not match.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That doesn't quite answer my question, which was: Do you remember the quote of Mr. Mesic that you were in the middle of telling the Court about yesterday? If you don't remember it, don't worry, just say so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be a good idea that if there are any questions from the Bench that they are put to the witness now so that then finally we can see whether there is anything for the parties to remain to be asked. I have the following question for you: Your attention was drawn a minute ago to the meeting on the 12th of September, 1991. You have said you -- I think you were not a member of the SDS. Let me just check that. Yes. You said you were never a -- were you ever a member of the SDS? The answer was no. Now, I read in this 12th of September, 1991 report the following, and I don't know whether you've got it in front of you. If you need it, please tell me. It reads: "In his opening remarks, Simovic emphasised the need to hold these kinds of meetings and that the practice should be continued in the future and that besides the SDS personnel and the ministries, SDS personnel from the judicial organs and certain events and agencies and the like should be invited to the meetings in future." Were you ever invited for these kind of meetings? I think you already told us that you were not at this meeting. Were you ever invited on these kind of meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not invited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Then I have one other question for you. Are you aware of the -- did that War Presidencies or War Commissions were created in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In municipalities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the municipalities, yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they existed in some municipalities, that they were established in some municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you explain to me what or whether you see any difference between War Presidencies or War Commissions, both in the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depends on the situation and on people's understanding. And as for major differences -- I suppose not both of these could be in keeping with the regulations. It would be more appropriate in Bosnia and Herzegovina to have had a War Presidency. A commission is not a word that was used in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So were these War Presidencies, did they have a basis in the legal framework of the -- of the republic, of the Serb republic of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina? I'm now talking about May, June 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were formed exclusively during the war. If you haven't got a war situation, then you couldn't form a War Presidency. It wouldn't be in conformity with the law, because the very term "War Presidency" means that it is something set up during the war. If there is no state of war, then there's no need for the existence of a War Presidency, and the regular organs would go about their business because it's considered that the regular organs company function in peacetime, and there's no need to set up a collective organ if all the other organs perform their duties. So the War Presidency is exclusively linked to a war. If there is no war, there's no need to set up a War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that a legal requirement that there was a state of war in order to form these War Presidencies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Precisely. There must have existed a situation of war pursuant to the provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I read that also in tab 6, which is the law on the amending -- the constitutional law for implementing the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which we were confronted with yesterday in relation to the expanded Presidency, at least a legal basis for such an expanded Presidency. Now, I read in this same Article 1, after paragraph 5, new paragraph 6 and 7 are added and read: "During a state of war, the Presidency may decide to establish War Presidencies in the municipalities." Is that what you were referring to a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. So as I said, there must be a state of war for War Presidencies in the municipalities to be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this creates the following dilemma for me, and please assist me to perhaps further clarify the matter: You testified that there could not have been an expanded Presidency because a state of war was never declared. You just answered my questions that War Presidencies were created in some municipalities. Now, the law requires a state of war for the establishment of such Presidencies, so you say on one hand an expanded Presidency could never be there is because a state of war was never declare; whereas for the creation -- or for at least for the establishment of War Presidencies you say this was a legal requirement as well, and you say they were establish. Do you understand my dilemma? Was the state of war there for the establishment of War Presidencies but not for the Presidency to become an expanded Presidency? How do I have to interpret this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May 1991 -- 1992, I'm sorry, the municipalities did the best they could, and probably some municipalities did set up War Presidencies. But when this area was regulated by war and constitutional law -- by laws, I'm sorry, by laws and constitutional laws, then there was one commissioner set up to follow the work of the municipalities and the decision was taken not to declare a state of war but for institutions to continue working regardless of the threat of war, which meant that the situation was this: The presidencies were abolished in the municipalities and the various organisations were asked to go about their business and take on the responsibility of carrying out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These commissioners, could they be sent apart from a -- the existence of a state of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could be sent on a special assignment if power and authority was not functioning in any given municipality. Then commissioners could be sent out to take measures to establish the structures of power and authority and see that the -- that civilian life went ahead and the civilian authorities went ahead with their work. So you could send a commissioner regardless of whether a state of war had been proclaimed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber has heard evidence about the appointment of war commissioners. Are you aware of commissioners being called war commissioners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. As far as I'm concerned, a commissioner is every commissioner. There's no distinction between a war commissioner or whatever. I don't know what other people understood by that. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And are you aware of the use of the term "War Commissions" rather than just "commissions"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of that. Otherwise, the language is rich. So people can use different terms and have them understand different things by different terms. So in Bosnia you had a conglomerate of three languages. Perhaps the same institution is called by some people the commission and by other people Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if we are talking about commissioners, would commissioners have the authority to establish War Commissions or War Presidencies in the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can't establish something when a state of war has not been proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for those answers. Mr. Tieger, I noticed that you may have some questions on a matter where you said you wouldn't fully understand at that moment the proceedings. But before doing so -- Mr. Josse, the witness is your witness. Is there any issue raised by the Bench which would cause you to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I thought Mr. Tieger should go first, but I can tell the Court I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Actually, I just have a question about another matter raised by Mr. Josse. Further cross-examination by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that regard, I will need to use a document that I only have -- happen to have one copy of here. I can provide it so all the parties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO, then, so that we can all have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is an intercepted telephone conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Simovic of September 28, 1991. I'll need to look at it on the ELMO, too, in connection with my questions, I think. If we look first at the bottom of page 2. Right. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, the question -- the questions I have arise in connection with those questions that Mr. Josse asked you about. First of all, let me explain the procedure. Perhaps that will help. There will be a document that will be placed on the screen so the parties can read it. That document is in English. Therefore, I will read aloud relevant portions of it so that you can hear the interpretation, and then I'll just have a question or two about that. I'll tell you first of all it's in connection with the questions that Mr. Josse asked you in connection with support by the SDS and your comment that the SDS supported you by not seeking another person to -- for your position after you were already occupying the position of Chief Inspector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I take it that it's not the same as in the binder and under tab 5 of your binder, because that's the same date and is same interlocutors, as far as I can see quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as -- insofar as I can see, Your Honour, tabs 4 and 5 unfortunately are the same document, and that's the conversation of August 27th, about a month before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although tab 5 says -- oh, yes, 27th. I apologise. I made a mistake. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, something I don't do personally very often. I do want to put something on the record. I don't object to this, but this is a highly irregular course. The questions I asked in re-examination were completely proper, in my submission, arose from cross-examination. This is a point that should have been dealt with in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what the issue is, whether -- we still haven't heard the question, so therefore it's difficult for us to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to take that point in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My thanks to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 2 Mr. Simovic says: "However, we, apart from Sipovac, Micevic, Brdjanin, but don't hold me to that, all our personnel are in. Even Kapetina got it. The thing that you signed for Chief Inspector so that we don't lose that position. And Mr. Karadzic says: "Yes." And Mr. Simovic answers: "Everything has been accepted. I mean" -- and if we turn the page, we continue. Dr. Karadzic: "Have I signed for Kapetina, have I?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMOVIC
utterances.text: "Yes, you have, or you haven't. I don't know. Maybe Rajko Dukic signed." Dr. Karadzic: "Probably. Maybe he now ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMOVIC
utterances.text: "We are afraid of losing him, you know." Dr. Karadzic: "Yes, that he does not start behaving again as ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMOVIC
utterances.text: "No. He was appointed general director last year." Dr. Karadzic: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMOVIC
utterances.text: "And he will not ... all our personnel appointed by the government can be relieved of their duties within 15 days. We are only about to start working. There are some I am not pleased with." Mr. Kapetina, my question is: Does that reflect some active course by the SDS in 1991 to ensure that you were retained in that position as opposed to simply not taking action to replace you, and is that essentially how the process worked in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did have the intention to actively retain me, but you must be aware of the fact that the SDS offered that to apply to dozens of people who were not members of the party. It wasn't stated that you have to be a member of the SDS, but a Serb to give support to the government -- to the party in power. So in state institutions, in legal institutions and so on. Not only Dragan Kapetina, and that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if there are no further questions, Mr. Kapetina, I'd like to thank you for coming to The Hague and to answer all the questions of both parties and the questions of the Bench. I can imagine that it may not have been easy for you to testify in this court, being taken back to a time where, as you told us, within your family life things happened that one would wish never to happen in anyone's family life. So, therefore, the Chamber appreciated very much your coming to The Hague, and we wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the very proper cooperation between the Trial Chamber, the Defence, and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first deal with the exhibits in relation to the witness Kapetina. Mr. Usher -- Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D118, Your Honours, the article from Narodne Novine dated 18 September, 1991. D119, the CD of intercept of conversation between Rado and Karadzic and Dragan Kapetina dated 1st July 1991. D1120, excerpt from Sefer Halilovic's book, "Cunning Strategy." D121, interview of 13 July 2004. D122, interview of 14 May 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I missed I don't know whether a number has been assigned, but what we find under tab 1, which is not translated, but which was used to ask the witness's comment is not on the list at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I noticed that as the registrar helpfully went through that list, and we're in something of a dilemma about that, Your Honour. I mean, it's a very long document. It would take a lot of public money for it to be translated, and we have some concerns about that in truth. Having said that, I would be anxious that at least the first and perhaps the second, third, and last pages be admitted in evidence, but if the Chamber was anxious to have a whole translation, then of course we will send it to the CLSS. I instructed the person dealing with that in our team not to do that until we'd had a direction from the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the suggestion is that four pages will be translated and that they'll be tendered and admitted into evidence. The purpose of the whole exercise, Mr. Josse, if I well understood, is to demonstrate that instructions or manuals in difficult times were not uncommon and that the 19th of December document is resembling to some extent this manual. That's what I understood the purpose to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, hearkening -- today I've been talking about previous procedures where I thought it furthered my arguments, so I'm going to recite or cite a previous procedure that I think applies here as well, and that is I think in the past we've translated only particular portions of documents out of necessity and submitted those and with the proviso that if anyone thought there was a reason to have the remainder translated that could be done. So I don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So then, Mr. Registrar, this document of which only a couple of pages -- Now, Mr. Josse, do you then tender the whole of the document with only four pages translated or just the relevant pages in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You will excuse my ignorance, Your Honour. I'm not sure what the Rules are. I thought I was able, under the Rules, to submit the whole document if it wasn't all translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I think you're right as a matter of fact. So that we -- then I take it you'll come up with a selection of the pages in B/C/S together with the translation of those pages, and perhaps we already provisionally assign a number to the relevant pages of this document. I take it that the cover page would be translated as well, so that the chronology is at least more or less intact. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be number D123, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 123. And that's then provisionally -- portions of this document provisionally be admitted, awaiting translation and further specification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, whilst I'm on my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And whilst we're dealing with this, we have got now clean copies of the Halilovic directive that is found at page 223 of his book. And perhaps I could hand those out to all concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, I didn't ask whether there were any objections against any of the other exhibits that were read by -- but I see you're nodding no so that answers my question. Then all the documents just read by Mr. Registrar are admitted into evidence; D123 only provisional. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution number P1036, intercept of conversation between Miodrag Simovic and Radovan Karadzic. P1037, parties in arms. P1038, press conference by Stipe Mesic. P1039, intercept of conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Miodrag Simovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's of the 27th of August, the first one being of the 31st of July, because we have two intercepts of conversations between Simovic and Karadzic. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1040, note of meeting between republican state organs and SDS of BiH. P1041, minutes of meeting of council of Hadzici dated 11th of April, 1992. P1042, announcement to the Serbian people of Hadzici re election. P1043, Milanovic accuses Krajisnik of plotting against Dodik dated 13th May 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we need another number for the last intercept the witness was confronted with. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1044, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1044, copies to be provided soon by the Defence. Before we move on to our next witness, I think we first should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I take it that you had an opportunity to briefly speak with the witness who has already given us the solemn declaration but who has not yet been assigned a pseudonym. It would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: D14, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D14, yes. Witness, we will address you as D14. Face and voice distortion are in place. That also means that we have to switch to the other. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that the solemn declaration that you've given is also valid for your testimony. You are still bound, of course, during the course of your testimony by the solemn declaration you're given. Oh, there's no translation. Could we just check that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can hear the interpretation. I have not been able to hear anything so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I said, and I'll just -- I just reminded you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the very beginning even where the questions were not about your real testimony but about the other matter we have discussed before, the protective measures. May I remind counsel to switch off their microphones once the witness has answered the question. Then please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour will have to guide me to some extent. I'm unclear as to the status of the proceedings at this precise moment. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are at this moment in open session but face distortion, voice distortion, and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right. So I need to deal with the sheet. Do I do that in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can deal with the sheet in open session if you invite the witness not to read what's on the sheet but just to look at it and to verify whether it's the correct name and date of birth of the witness. So he should not read it allowed. Examined by Mr. Josse:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look at this sheet. I'd like you to be given a pen, and I'd like you to put your date of birth on this sheet which already has your name upon it, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The pseudonym sheet would have ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D124 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The question is whether your name appears on it and whether you would be willing to write your date of birth on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the name is mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for any identifying matter, please apply for closed session, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you, D14, to tell the Court a bit about yourself, and to do that, I submit we need to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
